Introduction
This chapter discusses general guidelines and procedures for 
weighing large fixed-wingaircraft exceeding a takeoff weight 
of 12,500 pounds. Several examples of center of gravity (CG) 
determination for various operational aspects of these aircraft 
are also included. Persons seeking approval for a weight and 
balance control program for aircraft operated under Title 
14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 91, 
subpart K, 121, 125, or 135 should consult with the Flight 
Standards District Office(FSDO) or CertificateManagement 
Office (CMO) that has jurisdiction in their area. Additional 
information on weight and balance for large aircraft can be 
found in Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Advisory 
Circular (AC) 120-27, Aircraft Weight and Balance Control, 
FAA Type Certificate Data Sheets (TCDS), and the aircraft 
flight and maintenance manuals for specific aircraf

weighing system (OBAWS) that, when the aircraft is on the 
ground, gives the flight crew a continuous indication of the 
aircraft total weight and the location of the CG in percent 
MAC. Procedures are required to ensure the onboard weight 
and balance system equipment is periodically calibrated in 
accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. 
An operator may use an onboard weight and balance 
system to measure an aircraft’s weight and balance as a 
primary means to dispatch an aircraft, provided the FAA 
has certified the system and approved the system for use in 
an operator’s weight and balance control program. As part 
of the approval process, the onboard weight and balance 
system must maintain its certificatedaccuracy. The accuracy 
demonstration test is provided in the maintenance manual 
portion of the Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) or type 
certificate of the onboard weight and balance system.
The system consists of strain-sensing transducers in each 
main wheel and nosewheel axle, a weight and balance 
computer, and indicators that show the gross weight, the 
CG location in percent MAC, and an indicator of the ground 
attitude of the aircraft.
The strain sensors measure the amount each axle defl cts and 
sends this data into the computer, where signals from all of 
the transducers and the ground attitude sensor are integrated. 
The results are displayed on the indicators for the flightcrew. 
Using an onboard weight and balance system does not relieve 
an operator from the requirement to complete and maintain 
a load manifest.

Introduction
Weight and balance in aircraft is based on the law of the lever. 
This chapter discusses the application of the law of the lever 
and its applications relative to locating the balance point of a 
beam or lever on which various weights are located or shifted. 
The chapter also discusses the documentation pertaining to 
weight and balance that is furnished by the Federal Aviation 
Administration (FAA) and aircraft manufacturers.
Weight and Balance Theory

Weight and Balance Computations 
(Amateur-Built Aircraft)
A good weight and balance calculation is the keystone 
of flight testing an amateur-built aircraft. Accurately 
determining the aircraft’s takeoff weight and ensuring that 
the CG is within the aircraft’s design for each flightis critical 
to conducting a safe flight test
The aircraft should be level when weighed, spanwise and 
fore and aft in accordance with the kit manufacturer’s 
instructions, and should be in the level flight position. It 
is highly recommended that the aircraft be weighed in an 
enclosed area using three calibrated scales. Bathroom scales 
are not recommended because they are not always accurate.

Determining the Loaded CG of a 
Helicopter
The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity 
(EWCG) of a helicopter are determined in the same way 
as for an airplane. See Chapter 5, Single-Engine Aircraft 
Weight and Balance Computations. The weights recorded 
on the scales supporting the helicopter are added and their 
distances from the datum are used to compute the moments 
at each weighing point. The total moment is divided by the 
total weight to determine the location of the CG in inches 
from the datum. The datum of some helicopters is located at 
the center of the rotor mast, but since this causes some arms 
to be positive (behind the datum) and others negative (ahead 
of the datum), most modern helicopters have the datum 
located ahead of the aircraft, as do most modern airplanes. 
When the datum is ahead of the aircraft, all longitudinal 
arms are positive.
The lateral CG is determined in the same way as the 
longitudinal CG, except the distances between the scales and 
butt line zero (BL 0) are used as the arms. Arms to the right

butt line zero (or sometimes referred to as the buttock) is a

$$ (500) \times (96) \div (2) = 24,000 $$

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 22, the four steps for determining the balance point (or Center of Gravity/CG) of a lever are:

1.  **Measure the arm** of each weight in inches from the datum.
2.  **Multiply each arm by its weight** in pounds to determine the moment in pound-inches of each weight.
3.  **Determine the total** of all weights and of all the moments (disregarding the weight of the lever).
4.  **Divide the total moment by the total weight** to determine the balance point.

Weight and Balance Theory
Two elements are vital in the weight and balance considerations 
of an aircraft.
•	
The total weight of the aircraft must be no greater 
than the maximum weight allowed by the FAA for 
the make and model of the aircraft.
•	
The center of gravity (CG), or the point at which 
all of the weight of the aircraft is considered to be 
concentrated, must be maintained within the allowable 
range for the operational weight of the aircraft.
Arm 
The arm is usually measured and expressed in inches and 
refers to the horizontal distance between the CG of an item 
or object and the datum, a point from where all measurements 
are taken. Arms to the left of the datum are negative (–) and 
those to the right of the datum are positive (+). The datum is an 
imaginary vertical plane from which all horizontal distances 
are measured for balance purposes. The position of the 
reference datum varies by aircraft design and manufacturer. 
When the datum is located off of the lever and to the left, all of 
the arms are positive and computational errors are minimized. 
Note: When the datum is established ahead of the aircraft, for 
example at the aircraft nose, all of the arms are positive and 
computational errors are minimized.

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here are the flying problems caused by nose-heavy and tail-heavy loading:

**Nose-Heavy Loading (CG too far forward)**
*   **Increased Drag and Angle of Attack:** The downward tail load must be increased to maintain level flight, which has the same effect as carrying additional weight. This forces the aircraft to fly at a higher angle of attack and increases drag.
*   **Insufficient Elevator Authority:** At low takeoff speeds, the elevator may not produce enough nose-up force to rotate. On landing, there may not be enough elevator force to flare the airplane.
*   **Lengthened Runs:** Both takeoff and landing runs are lengthened.
*   **Difficulty Gaining Altitude:** It is more difficult to take off and gain altitude.
*   **Nose Drop:** The aircraft tends to drop its nose when the pilot reduces throttle.
*   **Higher Landing Speed:** It requires a higher speed to land safely.

**Tail-Heavy Loading (CG too far aft)**
*   **Instability and Recovery Difficulty:** The aircraft is unstable and difficult to recover from a stall.
*   **Flat Spins:** If the unstable airplane enters a spin, the spin could become flat, making recovery difficult or impossible.
*   **Susceptibility to Stalls:** A tail-heavy aircraft is more susceptible to stalling at low speed, which is a specific concern during the landing approach.

LSA is a category of simple, very basic, small, light-weight, 
low-performance aircraft, other than a helicopter or powered-

LSA as an aircraft with a maximum gross takeoff weight of

Based on the manual excerpts, balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC aircraft do not require weight and balance computations because **the load is suspended below the lifting mechanism**.

Specific reasons provided in the text include:

*   **Fixed Center of Gravity (CG):** For WSC and powered parachutes, the weight of the airframe acts through a single point (the wing attach point or hang point). Because the range over which the weight may act is fixed at the pendulum arm length, the CG remains constant regardless of fuel consumption or weight variations. Consequently, there is no CG range to calculate.
*   **Proximity to Hang Point:** In WSC aircraft, the rear seat position and fuel are located as close as possible to the hang point while the aircraft is in a suspended attitude, meaning load variations have little effect on the CG.
*   **Constant CG in Balloons:** For balloons, the CG of the gondola remains constant beneath the balloon envelope.
*   **Difficulty Exceeding Limits:** The CG range in these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG limits.

While computations are not required, pilots must still consult the POH or AOI for maximum takeoff weight and minimum/maximum seat weight limits to avoid structural damage.

Roll control on a powered parachute is achieved by changing

the length of steering lines attached to the outboard trailing 
edges of the wing. The trailing edge of the parachute is pulled 
down slightly on one side or the other to create increased 
drag along that side. This change in drag creates roll and 
yaw, permitting the aircraft to be steered.
Balloons
The balloon is controlled by the pilot only in the vertical 
dimension; this is in contrast to all other aircraft. He or she 
achieves this control through the use of lift and weight. 
Wind provides all other movement. The CG of the gondola 
remains constant beneath the balloon envelope. As in WSC 
and powered-parachute aircraft, there is no CG limitation.
Underestimating the Importance of 
Weight and Balance
Many pilots, from sport pilot to commercial pilot, tend to 
underestimate the importance of proper weight and balance 
of their aircraft. Load sheets are taken for granted and hasty 
calculations are made of the aircraft’s CG. Unfortunately, 
each year there are a number of accidents related to weight 
and balance issues. Many of these occurrences could have 
been avoided had more attention been given to weight and 
balance.

Weight and Balance
Aircraft such as balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC do 
not require weight and balance computations because the load 
is suspended below the lifting mechanism. The CG range in 
these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG 
limits. For example, the rear seat position and fuel of a WSC 
aircraft are as close as possible to the hang point with the 
aircraft in a suspended attitude. Thus, load variations have 
little effect on the CG. This also holds true for lighter-than-
air aircraft, such as a balloon basket or gondola. While it is 
difficult to exceed CG limits in these aircraft, pilots should 
never overload an aircraft, as doing so may cause structural 
damage and/or failures. 
Weight affects performance; therefore, pilots should calculate 
weight and remain within the manufacturer’s established 
limits at all times.
WSC Aircraft
WSC aircraft are one- and two-place aircraft that exceed the 
criteria of an ultra-light vehicle but do meet the criteria of an 
LSA. The definitionfor WSC can be found in 14 CFR part 1.

decreased power causes a descent. Due to this characteristic, 
the aircraft is basically a one-airspeed aircraft. Once again, 
because the CG is fixed at the attach point to the wing, there

Based on the manual excerpts, adding weight to a WSC aircraft creates a unique interaction between speed and trim speed:

**Effect on Trim Speed**
Adding weight **lowers the trim speed**.

**Reasoning**
While increasing weight generally creates an increase in speed and descent rate (similar to airplanes and powered parachutes), the WSC aircraft has a unique characteristic due to its flexible wing structure:
1.  **Wing Twist:** Adding weight creates more twist in the wing because the outboard leading edges flex more.
2.  **Lift Distribution:** This flexing results in less lift at the wingtips.
3.  **Nose-Up Effect:** The reduction in lift at the tips creates a nose-up effect, which causes the trim speed to lower.

Therefore, although the aircraft may experience increased speed due to the added weight, the specific aerodynamic response of the WSC wing (increased twist) reduces the trim speed.

The WSC aircraft has a relatively set platform wing without 
a tail. The pilot achieves control by shifting weight. In the 
design of this aircraft, the weight of the airframe and its 
payload is attached to the wing at a single point in a pendulous 
arrangement. The pilot, through the flight controls, controls the 
arm of this pendulum and thereby controls the aircraft. When 
a change in flight parameter is desired, the pilot displaces the 
aircraft’s weight by the appropriate distance and direction. 
This change momentarily disrupts the equilibrium between the 
four forces acting on the aircraft. The wing, due to its inherent 
stability, then moves appropriately to reestablish the desired 
relationship between these forces; the wing flexes and alter  
its shape. As the shape is changed, lift is varied at different 
points on the wing to achieve the desired flight parameters

Based on the manual excerpts provided, adding or removing an item from the **Comprehensive Equipment List** is considered a **minor alteration**, not a major alteration.

**Documentation Required:**
The only documentation required for this minor alteration is:
1.  An entry in the **aircraft maintenance records**.
2.  The appropriate change to the **weight and balance record** in the **POH/AFM** (Pilot’s Operating Handbook/Airplane Flight Manual).

**Note on Major Alterations:**
The manual distinguishes this from a **Major Alteration**, which requires work to be done by an FAA-certificated mechanic or repairman, checked for conformity by a mechanic with an Inspection Authorization (IA) or an authorized agent of an FAA-approved repair station, and documented via a **Repair Station record** and/or **FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration**.

The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity

Based on the manual excerpts provided, moving passengers from rows 1 and 2 to rows 8 and 9 changes the Beech 1900's Center of Gravity (CG) in the following ways:

*   **Direction of Shift:** The CG is shifted **aft**.
*   **Magnitude of Shift:** The CG shifts aft by **7.8 inches**.
*   **New CG Location:** The new CG is located at **fuselage station 300.7** (inches aft of datum).
*   **Weight and Moment Changes:**
    *   There is **no change** in total weight.
    *   The **moment index** increases by **1,155 pound-inches/100** (from 43,139 to 44,294).

**Calculation Details:**
The manual explains that this is calculated using the total weight shifted and the distance moved:
*   **Total Weight Shifted:** 550 pounds (300 lbs from Row 1 + 250 lbs from Row 2).
*   **Distance Shifted:** 210 inches (Row 1 moves from arm 200 to 410; Row 2 moves from arm 230 to 440).
*   **Formula Used:**
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{\text{Weight shifted} \times \text{Distance shifted}}{\text{Total weight}} $$
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{550 \times 210}{14,729} = 7.8 \text{ inches} $$

The new CG is determined by adding this shift to the original CG:
$$ \text{New CG} = \text{Original CG} + \text{CG Shift} $$
$$ \text{New CG} = 292.9 + 7.8 = 300.7 \text{ inches aft of datum} $$

The aircraft should be weighed inside a hangar where wind 
cannot blow over the surface and cause fluctuating or false

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here is the information regarding the generator set's batteries:

**Battery Voltage and Charging**
The generator set uses a **24 VDC** system. The batteries are charged by a **battery charging alternator** that is belt-driven by the engine. This alternator also supplies power to the generator set control system.

**Operation if Batteries are Removed**
The provided text **does not contain information** stating that the generator set can keep running if the batteries are removed.

However, the text does specify the following regarding battery dependency:
*   **Starting:** If the batteries are discharged, the generator set can be started using a **NATO slave receptacle** connected to a fully charged 24 VDC system. The slave cable must be removed after the generator set starts.
*   **Control Power:** The **battery charging alternator** supplies power to the generator set control system.
*   **Emergency Operation:** The **BATTLE SHORT** switch can be used to override safety devices for continued operation in an emergency, but this does not explicitly state that the generator can run without batteries.

**Conclusion**
While the manual confirms the use of a **24 VDC** battery system and provides a method to start the unit with discharged batteries, it **does not state** that the generator set can continue to run if the batteries are physically removed.

repeats.answer:
Yes, the generator set can be operated with minor oil or coolant leaks, provided they are classified as **Class I** or **Class II** leaks.

According to the manual (Page 38):
*   **Class I** is defined as "Seepage of fluid (as indicated by wetness or discoloration) not great enough to form drops."
*   **Class II** is defined as "Leakage of fluid great enough to form drops but not enough to cause drops to drip from item being checked/inspected."

The manual states: "Equipment operation is allowable with minor oil and coolant leakage (Class I or II) and is able to perform its combat missions."

**Important Conditions:**
*   You must consider the fluid capacity in the item/system being checked.
*   When operating with Class I or Class II leaks, you must continue to check fluid levels as required in your PMCS.
*   All leaks should be reported to the next higher level of maintenance.

**Note on Class III Leaks:**
The PMCS table (Page 45, Items 36 and 37) indicates that the equipment is **Not Fully Mission Capable** if there are **Class III** leaks (leakage great enough to form drops that fall from the item).

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 39, here is the explanation regarding the oily residue:

**Cause**
The oily residue (unburned fuel oil) appears because the **fuel injection system** is unable to consistently meter the small amount of fuel required when the generator set operates at **light loads** (specifically less than 25% of the set rating). The manual notes that this is not a defect in the fuel system.

**Removal**
*   **Operation at rated load:** Running the generator set at rated load will burn off the oily residue. The time required depends on the amount of residue present.
*   **Muffler cleaning:** If excessive build-up occurs, the **muffler** may need to be removed and cleaned.

**Prevention**
The oily residue can be prevented by **increasing the electrical load** on the set.

SECTION Ill . TECHNICAL PRINCIPLES OF OPERATION
1-10 
This section contains functional descriptions of the
generator set and explains how the controls and indicators
1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

Based on the manual excerpts provided, here is the procedure to slave start the generator set when its batteries are discharged:

1.  **Connect the Cable:** Connect one end of the **NATO slave cable** to a fully charged **24 VDC system** and the other end to the discharged generator set’s **NATO slave receptacle**.
2.  **Start the Engine:** Start the discharged generator set. Refer to **Paragraph 2-10** for the specific engine starting procedures.
3.  **Disconnect:** Remove the **NATO slave cable** after the generator set starts.

1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

performance of maintenance.  This list also includes parts which must be removed for replacement of the authorized

listed in ascending figure and item number sequence.  Bulk materials are listed in item name sequence.  Repair parts kits

Introduction
This chapter discusses general guidelines and procedures for 
weighing large fixed-wingaircraft exceeding a takeoff weight 
of 12,500 pounds. Several examples of center of gravity (CG) 
determination for various operational aspects of these aircraft 
are also included. Persons seeking approval for a weight and 
balance control program for aircraft operated under Title 
14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 91, 
subpart K, 121, 125, or 135 should consult with the Flight 
Standards District Office(FSDO) or CertificateManagement

information on weight and balance for large aircraft can be 
found in Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Advisory 
Circular (AC) 120-27, Aircraft Weight and Balance Control, 
FAA Type Certificate Data Sheets (TCDS), and the aircraft 
flight and maintenance manuals for specific aircraf

An operator may use an onboard weight and balance

The system consists of strain-sensing transducers in each 
main wheel and nosewheel axle, a weight and balance 
computer, and indicators that show the gross weight, the 
CG location in percent MAC, and an indicator of the ground 
attitude of the aircraft.
The strain sensors measure the amount each axle defl cts and 
sends this data into the computer, where signals from all of 
the transducers and the ground attitude sensor are integrated. 
The results are displayed on the indicators for the flightcrew. 
Using an onboard weight and balance system does not relieve 
an operator from the requirement to complete and maintain 
a load manifest.

Introduction
Weight and balance in aircraft is based on the law of the lever. 
This chapter discusses the application of the law of the lever 
and its applications relative to locating the balance point of a 
beam or lever on which various weights are located or shifted. 
The chapter also discusses the documentation pertaining to 
weight and balance that is furnished by the Federal Aviation 
Administration (FAA) and aircraft manufacturers.

A good weight and balance calculation is the keystone 
of flight testing an amateur-built aircraft. Accurately 
determining the aircraft’s takeoff weight and ensuring that 
the CG is within the aircraft’s design for each flightis critical 
to conducting a safe flight test
The aircraft should be level when weighed, spanwise and 
fore and aft in accordance with the kit manufacturer’s 
instructions, and should be in the level flight position. It 
is highly recommended that the aircraft be weighed in an 
enclosed area using three calibrated scales. Bathroom scales 
are not recommended because they are not always accurate.

Helicopter
The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity 
(EWCG) of a helicopter are determined in the same way 
as for an airplane. See Chapter 5, Single-Engine Aircraft 
Weight and Balance Computations. The weights recorded 
on the scales supporting the helicopter are added and their 
distances from the datum are used to compute the moments 
at each weighing point. The total moment is divided by the 
total weight to determine the location of the CG in inches 
from the datum. The datum of some helicopters is located at 
the center of the rotor mast, but since this causes some arms 
to be positive (behind the datum) and others negative (ahead 
of the datum), most modern helicopters have the datum 
located ahead of the aircraft, as do most modern airplanes. 
When the datum is ahead of the aircraft, all longitudinal 
arms are positive.

longitudinal CG, except the distances between the scales and 
butt line zero (BL 0) are used as the arms. Arms to the right

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 22, the four steps for determining the balance point (or Center of Gravity/CG) of a lever are:

1.  **Measure the arm** of each weight in inches from the datum.
2.  **Multiply each arm by its weight** in pounds to determine the moment in pound-inches of each weight.

4.  **Divide the total moment by the total weight** to determine the balance point.

Weight and Balance Theory
Two elements are vital in the weight and balance considerations 
of an aircraft.
•	
The total weight of the aircraft must be no greater 
than the maximum weight allowed by the FAA for 
the make and model of the aircraft.
•	
The center of gravity (CG), or the point at which 
all of the weight of the aircraft is considered to be 
concentrated, must be maintained within the allowable 
range for the operational weight of the aircraft.
Arm 
The arm is usually measured and expressed in inches and 
refers to the horizontal distance between the CG of an item 
or object and the datum, a point from where all measurements 
are taken. Arms to the left of the datum are negative (–) and 
those to the right of the datum are positive (+). The datum is an 
imaginary vertical plane from which all horizontal distances 
are measured for balance purposes. The position of the 
reference datum varies by aircraft design and manufacturer. 
When the datum is located off of the lever and to the left, all of 
the arms are positive and computational errors are minimized. 
Note: When the datum is established ahead of the aircraft, for 
example at the aircraft nose, all of the arms are positive and 
computational errors are minimized.

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here are the flying problems caused by nose-heavy and tail-heavy loading:

**Nose-Heavy Loading (CG too far forward)**
*   **Increased Drag and Angle of Attack:** The downward tail load must be increased to maintain level flight, which has the same effect as carrying additional weight. This forces the aircraft to fly at a higher angle of attack and increases drag.
*   **Insufficient Elevator Authority:** At low takeoff speeds, the elevator may not produce enough nose-up force to rotate. On landing, there may not be enough elevator force to flare the airplane.
*   **Lengthened Runs:** Both takeoff and landing runs are lengthened.
*   **Difficulty Gaining Altitude:** It is more difficult to take off and gain altitude.
*   **Nose Drop:** The aircraft tends to drop its nose when the pilot reduces throttle.
*   **Higher Landing Speed:** It requires a higher speed to land safely.

**Tail-Heavy Loading (CG too far aft)**
*   **Instability and Recovery Difficulty:** The aircraft is unstable and difficult to recover from a stall.
*   **Flat Spins:** If the unstable airplane enters a spin, the spin could become flat, making recovery difficult or impossible.
*   **Susceptibility to Stalls:** A tail-heavy aircraft is more susceptible to stalling at low speed, which is a specific concern during the landing approach.

LSA is a category of simple, very basic, small, light-weight, 
low-performance aircraft, other than a helicopter or powered-

Based on the manual excerpts, balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC aircraft do not require weight and balance computations because **the load is suspended below the lifting mechanism**.

Specific reasons provided in the text include:

*   **Fixed Center of Gravity (CG):** For WSC and powered parachutes, the weight of the airframe acts through a single point (the wing attach point or hang point). Because the range over which the weight may act is fixed at the pendulum arm length, the CG remains constant regardless of fuel consumption or weight variations. Consequently, there is no CG range to calculate.
*   **Proximity to Hang Point:** In WSC aircraft, the rear seat position and fuel are located as close as possible to the hang point while the aircraft is in a suspended attitude, meaning load variations have little effect on the CG.
*   **Constant CG in Balloons:** For balloons, the CG of the gondola remains constant beneath the balloon envelope.
*   **Difficulty Exceeding Limits:** The CG range in these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG limits.

While computations are not required, pilots must still consult the POH or AOI for maximum takeoff weight and minimum/maximum seat weight limits to avoid structural damage.

down slightly on one side or the other to create increased

Balloons
The balloon is controlled by the pilot only in the vertical 
dimension; this is in contrast to all other aircraft. He or she 
achieves this control through the use of lift and weight.

remains constant beneath the balloon envelope. As in WSC 
and powered-parachute aircraft, there is no CG limitation.
Underestimating the Importance of 
Weight and Balance
Many pilots, from sport pilot to commercial pilot, tend to 
underestimate the importance of proper weight and balance 
of their aircraft. Load sheets are taken for granted and hasty 
calculations are made of the aircraft’s CG. Unfortunately, 
each year there are a number of accidents related to weight 
and balance issues. Many of these occurrences could have 
been avoided had more attention been given to weight and 
balance.

Based on the manual excerpts, adding weight to a WSC aircraft creates a unique interaction between speed and trim speed:

**Effect on Trim Speed**
Adding weight **lowers the trim speed**.

**Reasoning**
While increasing weight generally creates an increase in speed and descent rate (similar to airplanes and powered parachutes), the WSC aircraft has a unique characteristic due to its flexible wing structure:
1.  **Wing Twist:** Adding weight creates more twist in the wing because the outboard leading edges flex more.
2.  **Lift Distribution:** This flexing results in less lift at the wingtips.
3.  **Nose-Up Effect:** The reduction in lift at the tips creates a nose-up effect, which causes the trim speed to lower.

Therefore, although the aircraft may experience increased speed due to the added weight, the specific aerodynamic response of the WSC wing (increased twist) reduces the trim speed.

Based on the manual excerpts provided, adding or removing an item from the **Comprehensive Equipment List** is considered a **minor alteration**, not a major alteration.

**Documentation Required:**
The only documentation required for this minor alteration is:
1.  An entry in the **aircraft maintenance records**.
2.  The appropriate change to the **weight and balance record** in the **POH/AFM** (Pilot’s Operating Handbook/Airplane Flight Manual).

**Note on Major Alterations:**
The manual distinguishes this from a **Major Alteration**, which requires work to be done by an FAA-certificated mechanic or repairman, checked for conformity by a mechanic with an Inspection Authorization (IA) or an authorized agent of an FAA-approved repair station, and documented via a **Repair Station record** and/or **FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration**.

The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity

The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity 
(EWCG) of a helicopter are determined in the same way 
as for an airplane. See Chapter 5, Single-Engine Aircraft 
Weight and Balance Computations. The weights recorded

of the datum), most modern helicopters have the datum 
located ahead of the aircraft, as do most modern airplanes.

arms are positive.

Based on the manual excerpts provided, moving passengers from rows 1 and 2 to rows 8 and 9 changes the Beech 1900's Center of Gravity (CG) in the following ways:

*   **Direction of Shift:** The CG is shifted **aft**.
*   **Magnitude of Shift:** The CG shifts aft by **7.8 inches**.
*   **New CG Location:** The new CG is located at **fuselage station 300.7** (inches aft of datum).
*   **Weight and Moment Changes:**
    *   There is **no change** in total weight.
    *   The **moment index** increases by **1,155 pound-inches/100** (from 43,139 to 44,294).

**Calculation Details:**
The manual explains that this is calculated using the total weight shifted and the distance moved:
*   **Total Weight Shifted:** 550 pounds (300 lbs from Row 1 + 250 lbs from Row 2).
*   **Distance Shifted:** 210 inches (Row 1 moves from arm 200 to 410; Row 2 moves from arm 230 to 440).
*   **Formula Used:**
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{\text{Weight shifted} \times \text{Distance shifted}}{\text{Total weight}} $$
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{550 \times 210}{14,729} = 7.8 \text{ inches} $$

The new CG is determined by adding this shift to the original CG:
$$ \text{New CG} = \text{Original CG} + \text{CG Shift} $$
$$ \text{New CG} = 292.9 + 7.8 = 300.7 \text{ inches aft of datum} $$

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here is the information regarding the generator set's batteries:

**Battery Voltage and Charging**
The generator set uses a **24 VDC** system. The batteries are charged by a **battery charging alternator** that is belt-driven by the engine. This alternator also supplies power to the generator set control system.

**Operation if Batteries are Removed**
The provided text **does not contain information** stating that the generator set can keep running if the batteries are removed.

However, the text does specify the following regarding battery dependency:
*   **Starting:** If the batteries are discharged, the generator set can be started using a **NATO slave receptacle** connected to a fully charged 24 VDC system. The slave cable must be removed after the generator set starts.
*   **Control Power:** The **battery charging alternator** supplies power to the generator set control system.
*   **Emergency Operation:** The **BATTLE SHORT** switch can be used to override safety devices for continued operation in an emergency, but this does not explicitly state that the generator can run without batteries.

**Conclusion**
While the manual confirms the use of a **24 VDC** battery system and provides a method to start the unit with discharged batteries, it **does not state** that the generator set can continue to run if the batteries are physically removed.

repeats.answer:
Yes, the generator set can be operated with minor oil or coolant leaks, provided they are classified as **Class I** or **Class II** leaks.

According to the manual (Page 38):
*   **Class I** is defined as "Seepage of fluid (as indicated by wetness or discoloration) not great enough to form drops."
*   **Class II** is defined as "Leakage of fluid great enough to form drops but not enough to cause drops to drip from item being checked/inspected."

The manual states: "Equipment operation is allowable with minor oil and coolant leakage (Class I or II) and is able to perform its combat missions."

**Important Conditions:**
*   You must consider the fluid capacity in the item/system being checked.
*   When operating with Class I or Class II leaks, you must continue to check fluid levels as required in your PMCS.
*   All leaks should be reported to the next higher level of maintenance.

**Note on Class III Leaks:**
The PMCS table (Page 45, Items 36 and 37) indicates that the equipment is **Not Fully Mission Capable** if there are **Class III** leaks (leakage great enough to form drops that fall from the item).

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 39, here is the explanation regarding the oily residue:

**Cause**
The oily residue (unburned fuel oil) appears because the **fuel injection system** is unable to consistently meter the small amount of fuel required when the generator set operates at **light loads** (specifically less than 25% of the set rating). The manual notes that this is not a defect in the fuel system.

**Removal**
*   **Operation at rated load:** Running the generator set at rated load will burn off the oily residue. The time required depends on the amount of residue present.
*   **Muffler cleaning:** If excessive build-up occurs, the **muffler** may need to be removed and cleaned.

**Prevention**
The oily residue can be prevented by **increasing the electrical load** on the set.

SECTION Ill . TECHNICAL PRINCIPLES OF OPERATION
1-10 
This section contains functional descriptions of the
generator set and explains how the controls and indicators
1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

Maintenance of the Lubricating and Servicing Unit.  It authorizes the requisitioning, issue, and disposition of spares,
repair parts and special tools as indicated by the source, maintenance and recoverability (SMR) codes.

following sections:
a.  Section II.  Repair Parts List.  A list of spares and repair parts authorized by this RPSTL for use in the
performance of maintenance.  This list also includes parts which must be removed for replacement of the authorized
parts.  Parts lists are composed of functional groups in ascending alphanumeric sequence, with the parts in each group
listed in ascending figure and item number sequence.  Bulk materials are listed in item name sequence.  Repair parts kits
are listed separately in functional groups in Section II.  Repair parts for repairable special tools are also listed in this
section.  Items listed are shown in the associated illustration(s)/figure(s).

authorized by this RPSTL (as indicated by Basis of Issue (BOI) information in DESCRIPTION AND USABLE ON CODE
column) for the performance of maintenance.

weighing large fixed-wingaircraft exceeding a takeoff weight

information on weight and balance for large aircraft can be 
found in Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Advisory

the transducers and the ground attitude sensor are integrated. 
The results are displayed on the indicators for the flightcrew. 
Using an onboard weight and balance system does not relieve 
an operator from the requirement to complete and maintain 
a load manifest.

Weight and balance in aircraft is based on the law of the lever. 
This chapter discusses the application of the law of the lever 
and its applications relative to locating the balance point of a 
beam or lever on which various weights are located or shifted. 
The chapter also discusses the documentation pertaining to 
weight and balance that is furnished by the Federal Aviation 
Administration (FAA) and aircraft manufacturers.

A good weight and balance calculation is the keystone 
of flight testing an amateur-built aircraft. Accurately 
determining the aircraft’s takeoff weight and ensuring that 
the CG is within the aircraft’s design for each flightis critical

The aircraft should be level when weighed, spanwise and

instructions, and should be in the level flight position. It 
is highly recommended that the aircraft be weighed in an 
enclosed area using three calibrated scales. Bathroom scales 
are not recommended because they are not always accurate.

Helicopter
The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity 
(EWCG) of a helicopter are determined in the same way 
as for an airplane. See Chapter 5, Single-Engine Aircraft 
Weight and Balance Computations. The weights recorded 
on the scales supporting the helicopter are added and their 
distances from the datum are used to compute the moments 
at each weighing point. The total moment is divided by the 
total weight to determine the location of the CG in inches 
from the datum. The datum of some helicopters is located at 
the center of the rotor mast, but since this causes some arms 
to be positive (behind the datum) and others negative (ahead 
of the datum), most modern helicopters have the datum 
located ahead of the aircraft, as do most modern airplanes. 
When the datum is ahead of the aircraft, all longitudinal 
arms are positive.

such as wind correction, heading and ground speed,

balance problems.

an E6-B can also be solved with a dedicated flight computer 
using the information shown in Figure 10-2. Each fligh

but all are programmed with prompts that solicit the required

formulas. Weight and arms are inputted as called for, and a 
running total of the weight, moment, and CG are displayed.

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 22, the four steps for determining the balance point (or Center of Gravity/CG) of a lever are:

1.  **Measure the arm** of each weight in inches from the datum.
2.  **Multiply each arm by its weight** in pounds to determine the moment in pound-inches of each weight.

Weight and Balance Theory
Two elements are vital in the weight and balance considerations 
of an aircraft.
•	
The total weight of the aircraft must be no greater 
than the maximum weight allowed by the FAA for 
the make and model of the aircraft.
•	
The center of gravity (CG), or the point at which 
all of the weight of the aircraft is considered to be 
concentrated, must be maintained within the allowable 
range for the operational weight of the aircraft.
Arm 
The arm is usually measured and expressed in inches and 
refers to the horizontal distance between the CG of an item 
or object and the datum, a point from where all measurements 
are taken. Arms to the left of the datum are negative (–) and 
those to the right of the datum are positive (+). The datum is an 
imaginary vertical plane from which all horizontal distances 
are measured for balance purposes. The position of the 
reference datum varies by aircraft design and manufacturer. 
When the datum is located off of the lever and to the left, all of 
the arms are positive and computational errors are minimized. 
Note: When the datum is established ahead of the aircraft, for 
example at the aircraft nose, all of the arms are positive and 
computational errors are minimized.

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here are the flying problems caused by nose-heavy and tail-heavy loading:

**Nose-Heavy Loading (CG too far forward)**
*   **Increased Drag and Angle of Attack:** The downward tail load must be increased to maintain level flight, which has the same effect as carrying additional weight. This forces the aircraft to fly at a higher angle of attack and increases drag.
*   **Insufficient Elevator Authority:** At low takeoff speeds, the elevator may not produce enough nose-up force to rotate. On landing, there may not be enough elevator force to flare the airplane.
*   **Lengthened Runs:** Both takeoff and landing runs are lengthened.
*   **Difficulty Gaining Altitude:** It is more difficult to take off and gain altitude.
*   **Nose Drop:** The aircraft tends to drop its nose when the pilot reduces throttle.
*   **Higher Landing Speed:** It requires a higher speed to land safely.

**Tail-Heavy Loading (CG too far aft)**
*   **Instability and Recovery Difficulty:** The aircraft is unstable and difficult to recover from a stall.
*   **Flat Spins:** If the unstable airplane enters a spin, the spin could become flat, making recovery difficult or impossible.
*   **Susceptibility to Stalls:** A tail-heavy aircraft is more susceptible to stalling at low speed, which is a specific concern during the landing approach.

LSA Definition of Term
LSA is a category of simple, very basic, small, light-weight, 
low-performance aircraft, other than a helicopter or powered-
lift, and a classification of aircraft specific to the United

LSA as an aircraft with a maximum gross takeoff weight of

Based on the manual excerpts, balloons, powered parachutes, and WSC aircraft do not require weight and balance computations because **the load is suspended below the lifting mechanism**.

Specific reasons provided in the text include:

*   **Fixed Center of Gravity (CG):** For WSC and powered parachutes, the weight of the airframe acts through a single point (the wing attach point or hang point). Because the range over which the weight may act is fixed at the pendulum arm length, the CG remains constant regardless of fuel consumption or weight variations. Consequently, there is no CG range to calculate.
*   **Proximity to Hang Point:** In WSC aircraft, the rear seat position and fuel are located as close as possible to the hang point while the aircraft is in a suspended attitude, meaning load variations have little effect on the CG.
*   **Constant CG in Balloons:** For balloons, the CG of the gondola remains constant beneath the balloon envelope.
*   **Difficulty Exceeding Limits:** The CG range in these types of aircraft is such that it is difficult to exceed CG limits.

While computations are not required, pilots must still consult the POH or AOI for maximum takeoff weight and minimum/maximum seat weight limits to avoid structural damage.

Balloons
The balloon is controlled by the pilot only in the vertical 
dimension; this is in contrast to all other aircraft. He or she 
achieves this control through the use of lift and weight.

remains constant beneath the balloon envelope. As in WSC 
and powered-parachute aircraft, there is no CG limitation.
Underestimating the Importance of 
Weight and Balance
Many pilots, from sport pilot to commercial pilot, tend to 
underestimate the importance of proper weight and balance 
of their aircraft. Load sheets are taken for granted and hasty 
calculations are made of the aircraft’s CG. Unfortunately, 
each year there are a number of accidents related to weight 
and balance issues. Many of these occurrences could have 
been avoided had more attention been given to weight and 
balance.

Based on the manual excerpts, adding weight to a WSC aircraft creates a unique interaction between speed and trim speed:

**Effect on Trim Speed**
Adding weight **lowers the trim speed**.

**Reasoning**
While increasing weight generally creates an increase in speed and descent rate (similar to airplanes and powered parachutes), the WSC aircraft has a unique characteristic due to its flexible wing structure:
1.  **Wing Twist:** Adding weight creates more twist in the wing because the outboard leading edges flex more.
2.  **Lift Distribution:** This flexing results in less lift at the wingtips.
3.  **Nose-Up Effect:** The reduction in lift at the tips creates a nose-up effect, which causes the trim speed to lower.

Therefore, although the aircraft may experience increased speed due to the added weight, the specific aerodynamic response of the WSC wing (increased twist) reduces the trim speed.

Based on the manual excerpts provided, adding or removing an item from the **Comprehensive Equipment List** is considered a **minor alteration**, not a major alteration.

**Documentation Required:**
The only documentation required for this minor alteration is:
1.  An entry in the **aircraft maintenance records**.
2.  The appropriate change to the **weight and balance record** in the **POH/AFM** (Pilot’s Operating Handbook/Airplane Flight Manual).

**Note on Major Alterations:**
The manual distinguishes this from a **Major Alteration**, which requires work to be done by an FAA-certificated mechanic or repairman, checked for conformity by a mechanic with an Inspection Authorization (IA) or an authorized agent of an FAA-approved repair station, and documented via a **Repair Station record** and/or **FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration**.

*   **Attitude and Rotor Pull:** The helicopter tilts, and the rotor disk generates a forward pull.

Helicopter
The empty weight and empty weight center of gravity

as for an airplane. See Chapter 5, Single-Engine Aircraft 
Weight and Balance Computations. The weights recorded

total weight to determine the location of the CG in inches 
from the datum. The datum of some helicopters is located at 
the center of the rotor mast, but since this causes some arms

of the datum), most modern helicopters have the datum 
located ahead of the aircraft, as do most modern airplanes.

arms are positive.

butt line zero (or sometimes referred to as the buttock) is a 
line through the symmetrical center of an aircraft from nose 
to tail. It serves as the datum for measuring the arms used to 
find the lateral CG. Lateral moments that cause the aircraft

Based on the manual excerpts provided, moving passengers from rows 1 and 2 to rows 8 and 9 changes the Beech 1900's Center of Gravity (CG) in the following ways:

*   **Direction of Shift:** The CG is shifted **aft**.
*   **Magnitude of Shift:** The CG shifts aft by **7.8 inches**.
*   **New CG Location:** The new CG is located at **fuselage station 300.7** (inches aft of datum).
*   **Weight and Moment Changes:**
    *   There is **no change** in total weight.
    *   The **moment index** increases by **1,155 pound-inches/100** (from 43,139 to 44,294).

**Calculation Details:**
The manual explains that this is calculated using the total weight shifted and the distance moved:
*   **Total Weight Shifted:** 550 pounds (300 lbs from Row 1 + 250 lbs from Row 2).
*   **Distance Shifted:** 210 inches (Row 1 moves from arm 200 to 410; Row 2 moves from arm 230 to 440).
*   **Formula Used:**
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{\text{Weight shifted} \times \text{Distance shifted}}{\text{Total weight}} $$
    $$ \text{CG Shift} = \frac{550 \times 210}{14,729} = 7.8 \text{ inches} $$

The new CG is determined by adding this shift to the original CG:
$$ \text{New CG} = \text{Original CG} + \text{CG Shift} $$
$$ \text{New CG} = 292.9 + 7.8 = 300.7 \text{ inches aft of datum} $$

Based on the provided manual excerpts, here is the information regarding the generator set's batteries:

**Battery Voltage and Charging**
The generator set uses a **24 VDC** system. The batteries are charged by a **battery charging alternator** that is belt-driven by the engine. This alternator also supplies power to the generator set control system.

**Operation if Batteries are Removed**
The provided text **does not contain information** stating that the generator set can keep running if the batteries are removed.

However, the text does specify the following regarding battery dependency:
*   **Starting:** If the batteries are discharged, the generator set can be started using a **NATO slave receptacle** connected to a fully charged 24 VDC system. The slave cable must be removed after the generator set starts.
*   **Control Power:** The **battery charging alternator** supplies power to the generator set control system.
*   **Emergency Operation:** The **BATTLE SHORT** switch can be used to override safety devices for continued operation in an emergency, but this does not explicitly state that the generator can run without batteries.

**Conclusion**
While the manual confirms the use of a **24 VDC** battery system and provides a method to start the unit with discharged batteries, it **does not state** that the generator set can continue to run if the batteries are physically removed.

The manual does not specify a particular component or circuit that the fuse itself protects; instead, it notes that the fuse's function involves **bypassing protective devices**.

repeats.answer:
Yes, the generator set can be operated with minor oil or coolant leaks, provided they are classified as **Class I** or **Class II** leaks.

According to the manual (Page 38):
*   **Class I** is defined as "Seepage of fluid (as indicated by wetness or discoloration) not great enough to form drops."
*   **Class II** is defined as "Leakage of fluid great enough to form drops but not enough to cause drops to drip from item being checked/inspected."

The manual states: "Equipment operation is allowable with minor oil and coolant leakage (Class I or II) and is able to perform its combat missions."

**Important Conditions:**
*   You must consider the fluid capacity in the item/system being checked.
*   When operating with Class I or Class II leaks, you must continue to check fluid levels as required in your PMCS.
*   All leaks should be reported to the next higher level of maintenance.

**Note on Class III Leaks:**
The PMCS table (Page 45, Items 36 and 37) indicates that the equipment is **Not Fully Mission Capable** if there are **Class III** leaks (leakage great enough to form drops that fall from the item).

Based on the manual excerpt from Page 39, here is the explanation regarding the oily residue:

**Cause**
The oily residue (unburned fuel oil) appears because the **fuel injection system** is unable to consistently meter the small amount of fuel required when the generator set operates at **light loads** (specifically less than 25% of the set rating). The manual notes that this is not a defect in the fuel system.

**Removal**
*   **Operation at rated load:** Running the generator set at rated load will burn off the oily residue. The time required depends on the amount of residue present.
*   **Muffler cleaning:** If excessive build-up occurs, the **muffler** may need to be removed and cleaned.

**Prevention**
The oily residue can be prevented by **increasing the electrical load** on the set.

The batteries are charged by the battery charging
alternator that is belt driven by the engine. Generator set
control system power is also supplied by the battery

indicates the charge/discharge rate of the batteries, from

SECTION Ill . TECHNICAL PRINCIPLES OF OPERATION
1-10 
This section contains functional descriptions of the
generator set and explains how the controls and indicators
1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

1-11 
The Engine Starting System (FIGURE 1-3), consists of
two 12-volt batteries connected in series, a starter, a 24
volt battery charging alternator, a magnetic pickup (for
sensing engine speed) and the related switches and
relays required for control of the starting system. For
engine cranking, battery power is supplied to the starter
motor through the starter solenoid which in turn is
controlled by the cranking relay. The starter then engages
the engine flywheel causing the engine to turn over. For
engine starting, the DEAD CRANK switch must be in the
NORMAL position, the DC Control power circuit breaker
must be pushed in, the EMERGENCY STOP SWITCH
must be in the OUT position, and the MASTER SWITCH
is moved to the START position. The cranking relay is
then controlled by a circuit consisting of the crank
disconnect relay and crank disconnect switch. As the
engine accelerates to the preset speed (sensed by the
magnetic pickup), the crank disconnect switch opens and
de-energizes the cranking relay to stop and disengage the
starter. The starting sequence may also be stopped by
moving the MASTER SWITCH to OFF. The engine may
be cranked without starting by use of the DEAD CRANK
switch. With the DEAD CRANK switch in the CRANK
position, the cranking relay, starter solenoid and starter
motor are energized without activating any other starting
or control function.

1.  SCOPE.  This RPSTL lists and authorizes spares and repair parts; special tools; special test, measurement, and

Maintenance of the Lubricating and Servicing Unit.  It authorizes the requisitioning, issue, and disposition of spares,
repair parts and special tools as indicated by the source, maintenance and recoverability (SMR) codes.

following sections:
a.  Section II.  Repair Parts List.  A list of spares and repair parts authorized by this RPSTL for use in the
performance of maintenance.  This list also includes parts which must be removed for replacement of the authorized
parts.  Parts lists are composed of functional groups in ascending alphanumeric sequence, with the parts in each group
listed in ascending figure and item number sequence.  Bulk materials are listed in item name sequence.  Repair parts kits
are listed separately in functional groups in Section II.  Repair parts for repairable special tools are also listed in this
section.  Items listed are shown in the associated illustration(s)/figure(s).

authorized by this RPSTL (as indicated by Basis of Issue (BOI) information in DESCRIPTION AND USABLE ON CODE
column) for the performance of maintenance.
